summary.verdict: Your page has evidence most outreach pages lack: a knowledge question with a right answer, counts for every option, and a question about the map itself. What holds it back is repetition and facts that do not match. The map and sound exhibit are described three or four times, the survey is presented as being about this booth when it covered the whole event, and several details disagree with each other or with the IHP and Geospatial pages.
strengths: Every survey result has a count, a base and a percentage, and the knowledge question has a right answer (32 of 62 picked Yilan).
You report a weak result honestly and turn it into a design target: the LED flashing was hard to read.
A real dialogue moment: visitors expected Taipei and asked why the data showed otherwise.
Clear science writing: the cited definition of data physicalization and the one-line explanation of cavitation.
Reusable detail in places: the data-to-element table, the listening website, and the headphones wired to laptops behind the poster.
priorities: Say once, at the start of the Impact section, that the survey covered all six booths, and mark which results are about the map. Then match the labels and categories to the IHP page.
Fix the facts that disagree: Yilan alone or Yilan and Nantou, the tourism explanation, “easy to see” against 32 of 62, the Figure 3 labels and caption, and the “most memorable” translation.
Describe each physicalization once. Move the build before the results, and cut 1.4, the repeated concept paragraphs and the repeats in the conclusion.
Name the data (crop, measure, years, source), the exact LED and color rules and the pitch shift, and add a build list so another team could make the board.
Close the loop: say what you changed or will change because only half read the map, and report the Instagram event with dates and numbers.

ballot.question: How well did their work promote mutual learning and/or a dialogue?
ballot.where: 3. Stress map: Public interaction; 2.1 (the design target)
ballot.note: Visitors’ surprise about Taipei and the half-right map reading are real dialogue, but the page never says what you changed because of them.

ballot.question: Is it documented in a way that others can build upon?
ballot.where: 3. Mapping data to physical elements; Sound of plants: Physicalization method (listening site)
ballot.note: The encoding table and listening site help, but there is no named data source, LED rule, materials list, code or pitch-shift setting.

ballot.question: Was it thoughtfully implemented?
ballot.note: The right-answer question is well designed, but the page credits the booth with results from a whole-event survey and never says when or where the booth ran.

ballot.question: Did the team convince you that their activities would enable more people to shape, contribute to, and/or participate in synthetic biology?
ballot.note: Synthetic biology appears only in a conclusion claim, and the Instagram event has no dates or numbers.

releaf: 1. Overview (goals, why physicalize, the data, from data to map)
winners: Purpose: why public learning matters, in one or two paragraphs
Structure statement: how the page is organised
Groups of activities, each opening with why this audience
Per activity: setting and headcount, what was taught, the hands-on part, how participants engaged, a measured or quoted outcome, what the team changed, materials to reuse
Forward look: who continues it and where the materials live
skeleton.gap: Your page reports impact before it explains how the map works, and it explains the map in both 1.4 and section 3. Winners keep each activity’s setting, build, engagement and outcome together, so open with the event, then each physicalization with its build and what visitors did, then the survey, then what you will change.

extras: Section 2.2: the line “95.2% of participants agreed our Data Physicalization Map helped them understand the relationship between climate change and crop yield.” repeats the sentence just above it. Cut it, or keep it and cut the number from the paragraph.
Sound of plants method cards: “Khait, Hadany et al.” but References: “Khait, I., Lewin-Epstein, O., Sharon, R., et al.” Use one form everywhere, e.g. “Khait et al. (2023) [1]”.
Sound of plants feedback: “some even mentioning how the sound physicalization was the most memorable part” should be “some even said the sound physicalization was the most memorable part”.
Conclusion: “Additionally according to our surveys, many people” needs commas: “Additionally, according to our surveys, many people”.
Section 2.1: “Yilan’s high stress amount was showcased through its frequent flashing of LED lights.” Write: “Yilan’s high stress was shown by its fast-flashing LEDs.”

Figure 2 caption: “Showcasing knowledge of the region with the highest stress.” does not say what was asked. Write: “Figure 2. Answers to ‘Which region has the highest plant stress?’ (n = 62). The correct answer, Yilan, is green.”

Figure 4: the chart shows “Selected at least one future sustainable action: 98 percent”, but the text never gives this number. Add it, e.g. “61 of 62 (98.4%) chose at least one action” (61 is the only count out of 62 that rounds to 98%).

Sound of plants concept: “how impactful it would be if the public realizes how plants can also sense stress” mixes tenses and overclaims. Write: “how much it would mean if the public learned that plants respond to stress”.

Event name: the page says “public forum booth” (Overview), “booth at our public forum” (Figure 1) and “public engagement booth” (Sound of plants). Your IHP page treats the morning forum and the afternoon booths as separate parts. Use one name, e.g. “our booth at the Water Garden Organic Farmers’ Market”.

notes.anchor: The picture shows our map physicalization being explained at our public forum booth.
notes.title: Open with what, where and when
notes.body: Your overview starts by describing a photo, so a judge does not yet know what the booth was, where it stood or who came. Open with the event, the two physicalizations and your numbers (the date and place below are from your IHP page). Also fix the grammar: “The different colors ... represents” should be “represent”.
notes.after: On 5 September 2026, at the Taipei Water Garden Organic Farmers’ Market, our booth showed plant stress in two ways: a map of Taiwan you could see and plant recordings you could hear. On the map, paper color shows crop yield, from dark green (highest) to brown (lowest). Red LEDs flash faster where plant stress is higher. [116] people visited the booth and 62 answered our survey.
notes.excerpt_note: Both openings tell the reader what was done and why in the first few lines, before any detail.

notes.anchor: As climate change intensifies, stress is often invisible to the general public.
notes.title: Say whose stress you mean
notes.body: On a page called “Stress data you can touch”, a reader may first think of human stress. Say plant stress, and name the kind (heat, drought). “To really feel the gravity of climate warnings” is also vague; say what people cannot see.
notes.after: Climate change is putting more heat and drought stress on Taiwan’s crops, but people rarely see it until the harvest drops. We built a map of Taiwan that visitors can see and interact with, so the link between climate, plant stress and crop yield is easier to follow than on a graph.

notes.anchor: is a physical artifact whose geometry or material properties encode data
notes.title: A cited definition before the term
notes.body: You define data physicalization with a quoted, cited sentence before you use the term again. A judge from another field knows exactly what you mean from the first line of the section. Wageningen, a 2025 winner, explains a trade term the same way.
notes.excerpt_note: Look at how “binders” is explained in the same sentence where it first appears.

notes.anchor: These visualizations help convey the data in a more accessible way (Jansen).
notes.title: Jansen is missing from your references
notes.body: You cite Jansen twice in 1.2, but the References list only has Khait et al. Add the full Jansen entry. This definition is usually traced to Jansen et al. (2015), “Opportunities and challenges for data physicalization”, CHI 2015; check that it is the source you used. The last sentence of 1.2 only repeats the definition, so you can cut it.
notes.after: - Jansen, Y., et al. ([year]). [Title]. [Where published]. [doi or link].

notes.anchor: Our selected datasets focus on crop yield and heat stress, making the data comparable across locations.
notes.title: Name the datasets, crop and years
notes.body: Section 1.3 explains how you chose data but never names it. Your IHP page says the map showed “heat stress and rice crop yields”, and Figure 4 on the Geospatial page uses nighttime temperature and rice yield for 2013 to 2016. If that is the board’s data, say so here. A judge cannot read a map without knowing the crop, the measure and the years.
notes.after: The board uses two county-level datasets: rice yield from [source, years] and heat stress, measured as [nighttime temperature], from [source, years]. We chose heat because it is one of the stresses ReLeaf protects against, and yield because it shows what that stress costs farmers.
notes.excerpt_note: Marburg says what the data had to do, then names the dataset and tools in two sentences.
notes.ballot: Is it documented in a way that others can build upon?

notes.anchor: The process of first acquiring the data, identifying its pattern, and turning it into a visual representation
notes.title: This sentence repeats the two before
notes.body: This sentence says again what the two sentences before it said, in more words. Cut it. Also cut the opening “Rather than selecting data solely because it was readily available” unless you name a dataset you turned down.
notes.after: We first found the patterns in the data that matter most for plant stress, then chose a physical feature of the map to show each one.

notes.anchor: We designed a physical map using styrofoam, colored paper, and LED lights
notes.title: Show the build before the results
notes.body: Section 2 reports how visitors read the map, but the build is explained in section 3. Section 1.4 and section 3 also describe the same map and sound exhibit almost word for word. A clearer order is Overview, Physicalizations (how you built each), Impact (what visitors learned), Conclusion. Then 1.4 shrinks to two lines.
notes.after: We built two physicalizations: a stress map of Taiwan and a plant-sound listening station. Section 2 explains how we made each one, and section 3 shows what visitors learned from them.

notes.anchor: many do not realize that plants can actually feel the impact of stress
notes.title: Plants do not “feel” stress here
notes.body: The paper you cite shows that drought makes water columns in the stem snap (cavitation), and that this makes a sound. It does not show that plants feel anything. “Feel” here, and “sense stress inflicted upon them” in the Sound of plants section, claim more than the research shows. Say that plants respond to stress, and that some responses make sound.
notes.after: Plants respond to stress in ways people cannot see. Few people know that a plant under drought stress makes sounds.
notes.excerpt_note: SDU limits its claim to exactly what was tested.

notes.anchor: After they visited our booth, we asked for them to fill out a form
notes.title: Say the survey covered the whole event
notes.body: This line says the form measured how much of “our booth” visitors understood. Your IHP page says visitors filled in one survey after collecting stamps at all six booths, and your Sound of plants section says visitors gave feedback “on the overall event”. Some answers (coffee, the ReLeaf device) came from other booths. Say this once here so judges know which results belong to the map. Also, “them” has no person to refer to.
notes.after: At the end of the event, visitors who had been to all six booths filled in one survey. 62 of the [116] people who visited our booth answered it. [Two] questions were about the map itself; the rest covered the whole event.
notes.excerpt_note: NYU says who was surveyed and how many before giving any percentage.

notes.anchor: 32 of 62 respondents (51.6%) correctly identified Yilan County, the region we represented as highest-stress.
notes.title: A real test, with every answer counted
notes.body: You asked a question with a right answer, and you give the count, the base and the percentage for every option, including the wrong ones (32 + 12 + 11 + 7 = 62). That is measured knowledge. Heidelberg, a 2025 winner, only measured self-rated knowledge and gave no number of participants.
notes.excerpt_note: NYU gives sample size, count and percentage together, as you do. Heidelberg shows how a result reads without an n.

notes.anchor: Just over half of visitors read the map correctly on a single, brief encounter
notes.title: Honest about a weak result
notes.body: You say plainly that only about half read the map correctly, and you turn it into a design target. Judges trust your strong numbers more when the weak one is on the page too. One tip: this is one 54-word sentence, so split it in two at “but”.
notes.excerpt_note: Heidelberg admits its pub quiz missed its audience and says what it took from that.
notes.ballot: How well did their work promote mutual learning and/or a dialogue?

notes.anchor: making the LED flashing-to-stress-level mapping more immediately legible
notes.title: Say what you will change
notes.body: You name the problem (the flash speed is hard to read) but not the fix. Close the loop with one concrete change and how you would check it. This answers the ballot’s mutual learning question: visitors’ answers changed your design.
notes.after: Next time, we will put a legend beside the board that shows [three] flash speeds and what each one means. We will then check whether more than [x]% of visitors pick the right region.
notes.excerpt_note: Each passage goes from what participants said to what the team changed, in two or three sentences.
notes.ballot: How well did their work promote mutual learning and/or a dialogue?

notes.anchor: the impact of climate change on Taiwan's coffee and crop production
notes.title: Same survey item, different labels
notes.body: The text gives three answers for this item: “very much understood” (39), “partially” (21) and not well (2). Figure 3 shows the same item as agree, neutral and disagree, and its caption says “impact of stress”, though the question asks about climate change. Your IHP page puts the same 62.9% under Knowledge (high and moderate understanding); this page puts it under Attitude. The question also names coffee, which came from the coffee booth. Pick one label set and one category and use them on both pages.
notes.excerpt_note: Counter-example: even a winner slipped here. Aachen gives two different view counts on one page.

notes.anchor: The physicalization itself was directly credited for this: 59 of 62 participants (95.2%) agreed or strongly agreed
notes.title: A question about the map itself
notes.body: This is the strongest evidence on the page: one question asks only whether the map helped, and you report the full spread, including the 2 neutral and 1 disagree answers. One small change: “for this” ties it to the result above, which other booths also shaped. Write “Visitors credited the map directly:”.

notes.anchor: several participants specifically pointed to the plant stress sounds rather than the map or spoken explanation
notes.title: Count the “several” and quote one
notes.body: “Several participants” is vague when you have 62 written answers. Give the number who named the sounds, and quote one; your Sound of plants table already has good ones. The last sentence (“doing real cognitive work, not just serving as ambience”) claims more than a few comments can show, so cut it.
notes.after: When we asked what was most memorable, [n] of 62 visitors named the plant sounds. One wrote “知道植物缺少水分的時候居然會發出聲音” (“I was surprised to learn plants make sounds when they lack water”). For these visitors, hearing the clicks made plant stress real.
notes.excerpt_note: A participant quote that states what she thought before and after, in her own words.
notes.ballot: How well did their work promote mutual learning and/or a dialogue?

notes.anchor: Together, these results trace a clear data of their understanding, awareness, and likelihood of future actions.
notes.title: End on what the data shows
notes.body: “Trace a clear data of” is not correct English. The next sentence (“left not just informed, but reporting an intention to change their own behavior”) also sounds stronger than a survey of intentions can support. Say what each part of the survey showed, and that these are plans.
notes.after: Together, the three parts of the survey show what visitors understood, how their views changed, and what they said they would do. Most said they would share what they learned and buy local or sustainably farmed food. [Say whether you followed up to see if they did.]

notes.anchor: Our data physicalization was inspired by the idea that scientific data should not only be seen, but also experienced.
notes.title: This repeats your Goals section
notes.body: “Invisible”, “tangible” and “accessible” all appeared in 1.1 Goals, so these two paragraphs mostly say it again. Keep the one new idea, the link to ReLeaf, and cut the rest.
notes.after: Plant stress starts inside the plant, where people cannot see it. Our booth made it visible and audible. This mirrors the core idea of ReLeaf: connecting hidden biological signals with information people can understand and act on.
notes.excerpt_note: Counter-example: even a winner made the same point twice in one paragraph. Cutting the second half lost nothing.

notes.anchor: We created the physical map using styrofoam as the base material
notes.title: Already said in 1.4
notes.body: This paragraph, and the sound paragraph below it, repeat section 1.4 almost word for word. Keep the full version here, with the color list and the table, and cut 1.4 to two lines. The last sentence of the LED paragraph also repeats the sentence before it.
notes.after: We built the map on a styrofoam base. Colored paper shows crop yield, and LEDs show plant stress.

notes.anchor: The frequency or amount of LED flashing increased with the severity of stress
notes.title: Frequency or amount: which one?
notes.body: “The frequency or amount of LED flashing” could mean faster flashing or more LEDs, and “intermediate colors” does not say which colors or how many yield bands. A reader, or a team copying your board, needs the exact rule. Also say what pattern visitors should notice: what color is Yilan, the county that flashes fastest?
notes.after: Each county has [n] red LEDs. They flash at one of [three] speeds: [speed] for low stress, [speed] for medium and [speed] for high. The paper comes in [four] colors, from dark green ([yield range, unit]) through pale yellow-green to brown ([yield range, unit]).
notes.excerpt_note: IISER reads one legend color aloud and says what it stands for.
notes.ballot: Is it documented in a way that others can build upon?

notes.anchor: We mapped each type of data to a physical or sensory element
notes.title: Add a build list others can copy
notes.body: Your table is a good encoding key. To answer the ballot question on documentation others can build on, add what another team would need: board size, number of LEDs, the controller and code, the data file, the cost and the build time.
notes.after: Materials: styrofoam board ([size]), colored paper ([n] shades), [n] red LEDs, [controller] running [code link], [power source]. Cost: [amount]. Build time: [hours]. Data file: [link].
notes.excerpt_note: CityU lists materials and steps for the next organiser; EPFL says exactly what its repository contains.
notes.ballot: Is it documented in a way that others can build upon?

notes.anchor: Many believed that regions such as Taipei would have the most stress instead.
notes.title: A real moment of dialogue
notes.body: This is the best dialogue evidence on the page: visitors expected Taipei, your data showed otherwise, and they asked why. Heidelberg won Best Education with the same move: a belief the public held, what the team showed, and what followed. Finish it by saying what you learned from their surprise.
notes.excerpt_note: One specific belief, what the team showed, and what the team concluded.
notes.ballot: How well did their work promote mutual learning and/or a dialogue?

notes.anchor: We explained the tourism in Nantou and Yilan were affecting its stress level.
notes.title: Yilan alone, or Yilan and Nantou?
notes.body: Your survey marks Yilan as the one highest-stress region, but this paragraph says “Yilan and Nantou had the highest stress”. The reason you gave visitors, tourism, is in none of the data on this page, and the Geospatial Analysis page links Yilan’s risk to warm nights in the rice belt. Check which counties the board showed as highest and what your data says causes it. Grammar: “curious on why” should be “curious about why”, and “the tourism ... were affecting its” should be “tourism ... was affecting their”.
notes.after: Many visitors expected Taipei to show the most stress and were surprised that [Yilan] did. When they asked why, we explained that [reason from your data, e.g. warm nights during the rice season]. Their surprise showed us that people tend to link stress with big cities, so we [what you changed or will change].

notes.anchor: The feedback we got that addressed the stress map was the fact that areas that receive stress were easy to see
notes.title: Easy to see? Your survey says half
notes.body: Here the high-stress areas were “easy to see”, but section 2.1 says only 32 of 62 picked Yilan and that the flashing should be “more immediately legible”. Both can be true, but say so. “Teach the Taiwanese public more about their own country” also claims more than one quote can show; the table below has one comment about the map.
notes.after: Some visitors told us the flashing made high-stress areas easy to spot, as in the comment below. Our survey shows this worked for about half of them: 32 of 62 picked Yilan. A legend would help the rest.

notes.anchor: Plants respond to stress in ways that are often invisible to the human eye until visible damage has already occurred
notes.title: Split this long paragraph, in time order
notes.body: This paragraph has five long sentences that mix the science, the idea for the booth and the link to ReLeaf. The next paragraph then tells how you found the paper, which happened first. Put events in order: the paper you found, what it showed, what you built. Use short sentences, and cite [1] where you write “recent research”.
notes.after: When we read Khait et al. (2023) [1], we learned that plants under drought stress make ultrasonic clicks, far above human hearing. We wanted visitors to hear them. The map let people see plant stress, and the recordings let them hear it. This matches ReLeaf’s core idea: stress can be detected before it turns into damage you can see.
notes.excerpt_note: HUST explains a specialist idea in plain words before it uses it.

notes.anchor: plants experience a physical process called cavitation, where continuous water columns inside the plant snap and form air bubbles
notes.title: A hard term explained in one line
notes.body: You name the process and explain it in the same sentence with an image anyone can picture: water columns snap and form air bubbles. A judge from any field can follow it. HUST and Wageningen, both prize winners, explain specialist terms this way.
notes.excerpt_note: Both explain the term at first use, in plain words, before building on it.

notes.anchor: we first collected plant sound recordings from scientists who had studied and recorded plants under different stress conditions
notes.title: Say where the sounds came from
notes.body: “Collected ... from scientists” sounds as if you contacted the researchers, but your References say the recordings come from Dryad, an open data archive, under a CC0 licence. Say that. Also say how visitors could hear them: Figure 6 puts the clicks at about 40 to 80 kHz, far above human hearing, and your listening site says they were pitch-shifted down. A judge will wonder how ultrasound came out of headphones.
notes.after: We used the open recordings from Khait et al. (2023), shared on Dryad under a CC0 licence [1]. The clicks are ultrasonic, so we shifted their pitch down by [factor] into the range people can hear. We built a website to play them, and at the booth two headphones were connected to laptops hidden behind the poster.
notes.excerpt_note: Marburg names its data source and tools in two sentences.
notes.ballot: Is it documented in a way that others can build upon?

notes.anchor: Most people had inquiries about how plants were able to make these noises in which we explained
notes.title: Question, answer, reaction, in order
notes.body: The first sentences are hard to follow (“had inquiries about how ... in which we explained”). The explanation here (“water would be hard to suck up”) also differs from the cavitation explanation above. Use one explanation in plain words, and end on what visitors said.
notes.after: Many visitors were surprised that plants make noise under stress, and most asked how. We explained that a dry plant pulls hard on the water in its stem, and the water column can snap and form an air bubble. Each snap makes a pop, a bit like bubble wrap. [One thing a visitor said or asked next.]
notes.ballot: How well did their work promote mutual learning and/or a dialogue?

notes.anchor: Hearing the crop's stress sound was the most memorable part
notes.title: The translation says more than the original
notes.body: 聽到作物的壓力聲音印象深刻 means that hearing the crop’s stress sound “left a deep impression”. It does not say “most memorable”. Section 2.2 builds on this answer, so keep the translation exact. Showing the Chinese next to the English is a good idea; just check each line. The line below also needs a subject: “I learned that plants actually make sounds when facing stress or danger.”
notes.after: Hearing the crop’s stress sound left a deep impression on me.

notes.anchor: Our data physicalization booth helped us achieve our goal of making plant stress and synthetic biology more accessible
notes.title: Cut the repeats and the synthetic biology claim
notes.body: The conclusion repeats the sound example and the survey from earlier, and “dire situation” is stronger than your data. It also says the booth made synthetic biology more accessible, but nothing on this page teaches synthetic biology. Either add one line on what visitors learned about it, or drop the claim.
notes.after: Our booth turned plant-stress data into something visitors could see and hear. In our survey, 32 of 62 found the highest-stress region on the map, and 59 said the map helped them understand the link between climate and crop yield. Next, we will [change to the board].
notes.excerpt_note: Counter-example: even a winner closed on a general claim a reader cannot check. End on a result or a next step.

notes.anchor: we began promoting a plant stress event where participants upload a picture of a stressed plant
notes.title: Give the Instagram event dates and results
notes.body: “We began promoting” does not say when, how many people took part, or whether it is still running. A judge asking whether your work lets more people take part needs those facts. Report numbers first, the way Heidelberg opens each section, or write it as a plan with a date.
notes.after: From [date] to [date], we ran a plant stress photo event on Instagram: people posted a photo of a stressed plant from their daily life and said why they chose it. [n] people took part, from [places].
notes.excerpt_note: Three one-line results, each with a number or a format, before the story.
notes.ballot: Did the team convince you that their activities would enable more people to shape, contribute to, and/or participate in synthetic biology?
